name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Shape and bond angle of trimethylamine

questiontext.text:
The diagram below depicts the molecular geometry and electronic structure of trimethylamine, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\):

Based on the diagram and the valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model, what is the hybridization of the nitrogen atom, the geometry of the molecule, and the value of the \(\mathrm{C-N-C}\) bond angle \(\theta\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The visual schematic presents a trimethylamine molecule featuring a central nitrogen atom with three bonded methyl (\(-\mathrm{CH_3}\)) groups and one unshared electron pair at the apex, subtending a base angle denoted by \(\theta\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Structural Model
According to valence bond theory and hybridization principles, nitrogen in amines forms three \(\sigma\)-bonds with carbon atoms and accommodates one non-bonding unshared electron pair. The steric number equals \(3 + 1 = 4\), dictating \(sp^3\) hybridization.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
An ideal tetrahedral arrangement of four electron pairs has a bond angle of \(109.5^\circ\). However, according to the VSEPR theory, lone pair-bond pair repulsion is significantly stronger than bond pair-bond pair repulsion. This unshared electron pair compresses the \(\mathrm{C-N-C}\) bond angle below \(109.5^\circ\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Due to the lone pair-bonding pair repulsion, the four orbitals adopt a pyramidal geometry rather than a planar or tetrahedral geometry. In trimethylamine, the experimental \(\mathrm{C-N-C}\) angle \(\theta\) is compressed to \(108^\circ\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The nitrogen atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised, the geometry is pyramidal, and the \(\mathrm{C-N-C}\) bond angle is \(108^\circ\).
Final Conceptual Answer: \(sp^3\) hybridised, pyramidal geometry, and \(108^\circ\).

answer.text: \(sp^3\) hybridised, pyramidal geometry, and \(108^\circ\)
\(sp^2\) hybridised, trigonal planar geometry, and \(120^\circ\)
\(sp^3\) hybridised, regular tetrahedral geometry, and \(109.5^\circ\)
\(sp^3d\) hybridised, T-shaped geometry, and \(90^\circ\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Hydration stability of substituted ammonium cations

questiontext.text:
The diagram below displays the extent of hydration via hydrogen bonding between water molecules and protonated alkylammonium cations (primary, secondary, and tertiary):

Considering only the solvation (hydration) effect shown in the diagram, what is the decreasing order of cation stability, and what order of basic strength of aliphatic amines would be predicted based solely on this factor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The visual representation depicts substituted ammonium cations in water: - Primary ammonium cation (\(\mathrm{RNH_3^+}\)) with 3 hydrogen atoms forming 3 hydrogen bonds to water molecules. - Secondary ammonium cation (\(\mathrm{R_2NH_2^+}\)) with 2 hydrogen atoms forming 2 hydrogen bonds to water molecules. - Tertiary ammonium cation (\(\mathrm{R_3NH^+}\)) with 1 hydrogen atom forming 1 hydrogen bond to water.

Step 2: Assumptions and Hydration Model
The basic strength of an amine in aqueous medium is directly related to the stability of the cation formed upon proton acceptance. More extensive hydrogen bonding between the cation and water releases greater hydration energy, thereby stabilizing the conjugate acid.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Stability of cation via hydration follows the number of available acidic hydrogen atoms on nitrogen capable of hydrogen bonding with water: \[ \text{Extent of H-bonding: } \mathrm{RNH_3^+} > \mathrm{R_2NH_2^+} > \mathrm{R_3NH^+} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since the primary ammonium ion has three hydrogens, it undergoes maximum solvation and stabilization, followed by secondary with two, and tertiary with only one. Therefore, considering hydration alone, the cation stability order is: \[ \text{Primary} > \text{Secondary} > \text{Tertiary} \] Consequently, if hydration were the only operating factor, the predicted basicity of amines would follow: \[ \text{Primary amine} > \text{Secondary amine} > \text{Tertiary amine} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Cation stability order by solvation: Primary > Secondary > Tertiary; Predicted basicity order based solely on solvation: Primary > Secondary > Tertiary.
Final Conceptual Answer: Cation stability order: \(\mathrm{1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ}\); Predicted amine basicity: \(\mathrm{1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ}\).

answer.text: Cation stability: \(\mathrm{1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ}\); Predicted amine basicity: \(\mathrm{1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ}\)
Cation stability: \(\mathrm{3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ}\); Predicted amine basicity: \(\mathrm{3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ}\)
Cation stability: \(\mathrm{2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ}\); Predicted amine basicity: \(\mathrm{2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ}\)
Cation stability: \(\mathrm{1^\circ > 3^\circ > 2^\circ}\); Predicted amine basicity: \(\mathrm{1^\circ > 3^\circ > 2^\circ}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Resonance stabilization of aniline versus anilinium ion

questiontext.text:
The diagram below displays the resonance contributors for unprotonated aniline (Structures I–V) and the protonated anilinium ion (Structures VI–VII):

Based on these resonance representations, which statement accurately accounts for the relative basic strength of aniline compared to ammonia and aliphatic amines?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The visual representation shows: - Unprotonated aniline has five resonance structures (I through V), wherein the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalized into the ortho and para positions of the aromatic ring, giving partial double bond character to the \(\mathrm{C-N}\) bond. - The protonated anilinium ion has only two Kekule resonating structures (VI and VII) because the nitrogen lone pair is bound to a proton and can no longer participate in resonance with the benzene ring.

Step 2: Principles of Resonance and Relative Stability
Thermodynamic stability increases with the number of significant resonance contributors. Aniline has five resonance contributors, while the anilinium ion has only two. Consequently, aniline is substantially more stabilized by resonance than its conjugate acid (anilinium ion).

Step 3: Basicity Determination
Protonation of aniline disrupts the extensive delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the ring, which represents a net loss of resonance stabilization. In addition, delocalization reduces electron density on the nitrogen atom, rendering the lone pair less accessible for protonation.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In aliphatic amines and ammonia, the lone pair on nitrogen is localized and readily available for donation. In aniline, because aniline is more resonance-stabilized than anilinium ion and the nitrogen electron density is diminished, proton acceptance is significantly lower. Thus, aniline is a much weaker base than both ammonia and aliphatic amines.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Aniline is a weaker base because resonance stabilizes aniline (5 structures) more than the anilinium ion (2 structures), and the unshared pair is delocalized into the ring.
Final Conceptual Answer: Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia because the free amine has five resonance structures and is more stable than the anilinium ion (which has only two structures).

answer.text: Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia because the free amine has five resonance structures and is more stable than the anilinium ion (which has only two structures)
Aniline is a stronger base than ammonia because negative charge accumulates on the aromatic ring, increasing proton affinity
Aniline and anilinium ion have equal resonance stabilization, making its basicity identical to cyclohexylamine
Aniline is a stronger base than aliphatic amines because the aromatic ring exerts a strong \(+I\) inductive effect

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Reaction intermediates in Gabriel phthalimide synthesis

questiontext.text:
The following reaction roadmap outlines the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis of primary amines:

Identify intermediate [Compound Q] and the [Amine Product], and choose the correct explanation for why aniline cannot be prepared by replacing \(\mathrm{R-X}\) with chlorobenzene:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The flowchart depicts the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: - Starting material: Phthalimide - Reaction with ethanolic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) forms potassium phthalimide [Compound P] - Reaction of [Compound P] with \(\mathrm{R-X}\) yields [Compound Q] - Alkaline hydrolysis of [Compound Q] with aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) yields sodium phthalate and an [Amine Product].

Step 2: Identification of Intermediates
The nucleophilic phthalimide anion formed in the first step attacks the alkyl halide (\(\mathrm{R-X}\)) via an \(S_N2\) nucleophilic substitution, replacing the halide to yield \(N\)-alkylphthalimide as [Compound Q]. Subsequent alkaline hydrolysis cleaves both imide \(\mathrm{C-N}\) bonds to produce the corresponding primary aliphatic amine (\(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\)).

Step 3: Reason Why Aryl Halides Cannot Be Used
Aromatic primary amines like aniline (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)) cannot be prepared by this method because aryl halides (such as chlorobenzene) do not undergo nucleophilic substitution (\(S_N2\)) with the nucleophile formed by phthalimide. This inertness arises from the resonance delocalization of the halogen lone pair into the aromatic ring, giving partial double bond character to the carbon–halogen bond, alongside steric hindrance and instability of phenyl cations.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- [Compound Q] is \(N\)-alkylphthalimide. - [Amine Product] is \(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\) (primary aliphatic amine). - Aryl halides cannot undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
[Compound Q] is \(N\)-alkylphthalimide; [Amine Product] is primary amine (\(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\)); aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.
Final Conceptual Answer: [Compound Q] = \(N\)-alkylphthalimide, [Amine Product] = \(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\), and aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.

answer.text: [Compound Q] is \(N\)-alkylphthalimide; [Amine Product] is \(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\); aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion
[Compound Q] is \(N\)-alkylphthalamic acid; [Amine Product] is \(\mathrm{R_2NH}\); aryl halides react too vigorously causing polyalkylation
[Compound Q] is \(N\)-alkylphthalimide; [Amine Product] is \(\mathrm{R_3N}\); aryl halides polymerize under alkaline conditions
[Compound Q] is phthalic anhydride; [Amine Product] is \(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\); aromatic amines are oxidised by potassium hydroxide

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Direct nitration of aniline yielding meta product

questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents the direct nitration of aniline using a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulphuric acid at \(288\text{ K}\):

Identify products P, Q, and R, and deduce the primary chemical reason for the substantial formation (\(47\%\)) of product Q:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Direct nitration of aniline with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at \(288\text{ K}\) produces three isomeric nitroanilines: - Product P: \(51\%\) yield - Product Q: \(47\%\) yield - Product R: \(2\%\) yield.

Step 2: Identification of Products
From the stereochemical positions: - Product P is \(p\)-nitroaniline (\(51\%\)). - Product Q is \(m\)-nitroaniline (\(47\%\)). - Product R is \(o\)-nitroaniline (\(2\%\)).

Step 3: Chemical Principles Governing Product Distribution
The amino group (\(-\mathrm{NH_2}\)) is normally a powerful activating and ortho/para-directing group due to resonance. However, nitration is carried out in a strongly acidic medium containing concentrated sulphuric acid.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Mechanistic Explanation
In the strongly acidic environment, the basic amino group of aniline accepts a proton to form the anilinium ion: \[ \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2 + H^+ \rightleftharpoons C_6H_5NH_3^+} \] The anilinium ion (\(-\mathrm{NH_3^+}\)) carries a positive charge directly adjacent to the ring. Through strong \(-I\) inductive electron withdrawal, it deactivates the aromatic ring and directs incoming nitronium ion (\(\mathrm{NO_2^+}\)) electrophiles predominantly to the meta position. Because an equilibrium exists between unprotonated aniline and the anilinium ion under these conditions, nitration of the anilinium ion leads to a significant amount (\(47\%\)) of \(m\)-nitroaniline.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
P is \(p\)-nitroaniline, Q is \(m\)-nitroaniline, R is \(o\)-nitroaniline; Q is formed in significant yield because aniline is protonated in strongly acidic medium to form the meta-directing anilinium ion.
Final Conceptual Answer: P = \(p\)-nitroaniline, Q = \(m\)-nitroaniline, R = \(o\)-nitroaniline; Q is formed because in strong acid, aniline is protonated to form anilinium ion, which is meta-directing.

answer.text: P = \(p\)-nitroaniline, Q = \(m\)-nitroaniline, R = \(o\)-nitroaniline; Q is formed because in strong acid, aniline is protonated to form the meta-directing anilinium ion
P = \(o\)-nitroaniline, Q = \(m\)-nitroaniline, R = \(p\)-nitroaniline; Q is formed because the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group steric hindrance blocks the para position
P = \(p\)-nitroaniline, Q = \(o\)-nitroaniline, R = \(m\)-nitroaniline; Q is formed due to intramolecular hydrogen bonding between \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) and \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\)
P = \(m\)-nitroaniline, Q = \(p\)-nitroaniline, R = \(o\)-nitroaniline; Q is formed because nitric acid oxidises aniline to nitrobenzene first

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_DIAGRAM_Q06 - Multistep synthesis of 2-bromobenzoic acid from 4-nitrotoluene

questiontext.text:
The reaction roadmap below outlines the synthesis of 2-bromobenzoic acid starting from 4-nitrotoluene:

Identify intermediate [Comp. A] and [Reagent D] required to accomplish this conversion:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The scheme shows the transformation of 4-nitrotoluene into 2-bromobenzoic acid: - Initial bromination of 4-nitrotoluene gives [Comp. A]. - Reduction with \(\mathrm{Sn/HCl}\) gives 3-bromo-4-methylaniline. - Diazotisation with \(\mathrm{NaNO_2/HCl}\) at \(273\text{--}278\text{ K}\) affords diazonium salt [Comp. C]. - Treatment of [Comp. C] with [Reagent D] yields 2-bromotoluene. - Oxidation of 2-bromotoluene with alkaline \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) gives 2-bromobenzoic acid.

Step 2: Analysis of Bromination (Formation of Compound A)
In 4-nitrotoluene, the methyl group (\(-\mathrm{CH_3}\)) is activating and ortho/para-directing, while the nitro group (\(-\mathrm{NO_2}\)) is deactivating and meta-directing. Both the directing effects reinforce each other to direct electrophilic bromination to the position ortho to the methyl group (which is also meta to the nitro group). Thus, bromination of 4-nitrotoluene yields 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene as [Comp. A].

Step 3: Reduction and Diazotisation
Reduction of 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene by \(\mathrm{Sn/HCl}\) selectively reduces the nitro group to an amino group, giving 3-bromo-4-methylaniline. Subsequent treatment with \(\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}\) at \(273\text{--}278\text{ K}\) converts the primary aromatic amine into the diazonium chloride, giving 3-bromo-4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride as [Comp. C].

Step 4: Deamination (Role of Reagent D)
To remove the diazonium moiety and replace it with hydrogen (reductive deamination) to obtain 2-bromotoluene, the diazonium salt [Comp. C] must be reduced using hypophosphorous acid and water (\(\mathrm{H_3PO_2 + H_2O}\)) or ethanol (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
[Comp. A] is 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene; [Reagent D] is \(\mathrm{H_3PO_2 + H_2O}\) (or \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\)).
Final Conceptual Answer: [Comp. A] is 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene, and [Reagent D] is \(\mathrm{H_3PO_2 / H_2O}\).

answer.text: [Comp. A] is 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene; [Reagent D] is \(\mathrm{H_3PO_2 / H_2O}\)
[Comp. A] is 3-bromo-4-nitrotoluene; [Reagent D] is \(\mathrm{Cu_2Br_2 / HBr}\)
[Comp. A] is 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene; [Reagent D] is \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\)
[Comp. A] is 4-bromo-2-nitrotoluene; [Reagent D] is \(\mathrm{HBF_4}\)
